par_001: You can recognise it by the concrete props under its heaviest branches and the ivy over most of the trunk, inside a low fence. It stands in Square Rene-Viviani, facing Notre-Dame across the quay.
par_002: You can recognise it by the flat, spreading crown visible right across the garden and the plaque at its base giving the planting date. It stands on the slope of the Grand Labyrinth in the Jardin des Plantes.
par_003: You can recognise it by the propped, scarred trunk that still flowers each spring. It stands in the allee beside the Ecole de Botanique in the Jardin des Plantes, grown from a cutting off the robinier at Square Rene-Viviani.
par_004: You can recognise it by the wide, mottled trunk of an oriental plane carrying the national Remarkable Tree label. It stands by the plane alley in the Jardin des Plantes, near the Rue Geoffroy-Saint-Hilaire gate.
par_005: You can recognise it by the trunk, 6.45 metres round, and by a first branch that starts higher than the park lampposts. It stands in Parc Monceau, the thickest tree in Paris and the largest oriental plane in the city.
par_006: You can recognise it by the height, over 30 metres and the tallest tree in Paris, on a trunk 5.53 metres round. It stands in the Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, well above the leaning pagoda tree down at the lake edge.
par_007: You can recognise it by the elm motif worked into the wrought iron balconies of the buildings around it, repeating the tree in the square. It stands alone in front of the Saint-Gervais church on Place Saint-Gervais.
par_008: You can recognise it by the fluted, muscular trunk, 4.45 metres round under 27 metres of crown. It stands on the side lawn of Avenue Foch's lower stretch, near Porte Dauphine, off the main carriageway.
par_009: You can recognise it by the trunk, 6.70 metres round and 30 metres tall, the heavyweight of the 14th arrondissement. It stands in Parc Montsouris, which was landscaped around it in the 1860s.
par_010: You can recognise it by the low, twisting trunk leaning out over the water, four metres round on a tree only twelve metres tall. It stands at the Buttes-Chaumont lake edge, under the artificial cliff.
par_013: You can recognise it by the trunk, 2.67 metres round and 20 metres tall, on a Caucasian elm rather than a true elm. It stands in Square Samuel Paty on Place Paul Painleve, facing the Sorbonne.
par_015: You can recognise it by the girth, 380 centimetres, which is what the register uses to pick this plane out of the several old ones along the quay. It stands in the Jardin Tino-Rossi sculpture garden on Quai Saint-Bernard.
par_016: You can recognise it by the shape, a low dome barely three metres high in summer and a tangle of spiralling, down-turned branches once the leaves drop. It stands in the square around the Roman arena of Lutetia.
par_017: You can recognise it by how slim it is, a metre round and still young where the register's other trees are giants. It stands in the Jardin Anne Frank off Impasse Berthaud, past the names inscribed at the entrance.
par_018: You can recognise it by a fig standing ten metres tall in the open, trunk 145 centimetres round, where figs this far north are usually trained flat on a wall. It stands among the carved stone fragments in Square Georges Cain.
par_019: You can recognise it by a giant sequoia only 19 metres tall, trunk 3.6 metres round, small for its species and weakening on the side facing Concorde. It stands in the Champs-Elysees gardens near the allee Marcel Proust.
par_021: You can recognise it by the evergreen leaves, glossy above and rust-brown felt underneath, on a magnolia standing free at twelve metres. It stands in Square d'Ajaccio, forty five metres from the square's registered plane.
par_022: You can recognise it by the trunk, 490 centimetres round and 25 metres tall, and by bark shedding in camouflage plates each summer. It stands in Square d'Ajaccio, forty five metres from the evergreen magnolia.
par_023: You can recognise it by a hazel grown as a single straight trunk, 235 centimetres round, under a tidy cone of a crown sixteen metres up. It stands in Square du Temple, the old Templar enclosure off Rue de Bretagne.
par_024: You can recognise it by the bark, shed once a year in pale corky strips more like a birch than a nut tree, on a trunk 265 centimetres round. It stands in Square Maurice-Gardette beside an olive, a ginkgo and a chestnut.
par_025: You can recognise it by the clean single trunk, 3.8 metres round under 26 metres, and in high summer by chains of winged nutlets half a metre long. It stands in front of the church of La Trinite, at the top of the metro steps.
par_026: You can recognise it in winter by the hard pale yellow berries hanging on bare twigs, and in summer by sprays of small mauve flowers. It stands in Square Boucicaut, facing the Bon Marche across Rue de Babylone.
par_033: You can recognise it by the acorns wrapped in shaggy, moss-like cups, on a trunk 190 centimetres round and 18 metres tall. It stands in Square Rene-Le Gall, 300 metres from the horse chestnut near the obelisk.
